recorded: 11 April 1950, Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York; LP published 1951
question: What happens when a tightly sprung dance interrupts a grand romantic gesture?
intro: Debussy’s original title names a doll based on an anti-Black caricature. The dance’s clipped rhythms meet a slower, extravagantly expressive middle; listen for how the jaunty opening regains control.

sections.label: A · The clipped dance
sections.mNote: syncopated melody moves against a regular bass-and-chord accompaniment

sections.label: B · An expressive interruption
sections.mNote: slower chromatic phrases alternate with short grace-note replies

sections.label: A′ · The dance restored
sections.mNote: the original tempo, accompaniment and dance material return

cues.title: A spring against the beat
cues.text: The lower part establishes a regular bass-and-chord pattern while the melody places accents and held notes across it. Listen to the friction between that steady support and the tune’s syncopation; the rests help make the dance feel sharply articulated.
cues.evidence: Viewed Durand score, printed pp. 24–25: Allegro giusto, syncopated melody, bass-and-chord accompaniment, rests and très net et très sec. The report’s opening grows to stronger windows around 0:20–0:25. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A dance crosses the Atlantic
cues.text: The cakewalk was an African American dance before it became a Parisian fashion. Black touring performers helped bring it to Paris around 1902–03. Debussy’s miniature belongs to that encounter, whose entertainment industry also traded in racial stereotypes.
cues.evidence: James Deaville discusses the dance’s African American origins, the Florida Creole Girls and other performers in Paris, and the racial context of Debussy’s piece: https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol2-n1/debussy-s-cakewalk/. No claim is made that Debussy attended a particular performance.

cues.title: Tristan enters the dance
cues.text: The slower middle alludes to the opening of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde. Debussy marks the lyrical phrase “with great emotion”, then sets it against short, detached replies. Listen for the contrast between expansive romantic expression and the dance’s smaller, sharper gestures.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 26–27 shows the chromatic lyrical phrase, avec une grande émotion and contrasting grace-note replies. Deaville identifies the Tristan allusion: https://revuemusicaleoicrm.org/rmo-vol2-n1/debussy-s-cakewalk/. The report’s strongest change at 0:52 and contrasting middle levels anchor the passage; the cue does not date the first quoted note.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The historical title’s racist image
cues.text: Florence Kate Upton introduced the Golliwogg in an 1895 picture book, drawing on a blackface minstrel doll. The original title is retained here to identify Debussy’s work, not to treat the racist caricature as innocent or to replace it with an invented title.
cues.evidence: David Pilgrim’s Jim Crow Museum account documents Upton’s 1895 character and its basis in a minstrel doll: https://jimcrowmuseum.ferris.edu/golliwog/homepage.htm. The viewed Durand score prints Golliwogg’s Cake-Walk. The historical wording is contextualised rather than silently euphemised.

cues.title: The dance takes over again
cues.text: The return recovers the opening’s quick, dry exchanges and regular accompaniment. Remember the middle’s lingering phrases as you listen: the same clipped rhythms now sound like a decisive answer to that interruption, before the abrupt final chords.
cues.evidence: Viewed score pp. 27–28 restores 1° Tempo and the opening dance material, ending with separated forte chords. The report marks a strong change at 2:00 and renewed high levels at 2:05–2:10, then a withdrawal after 2:30. The cue describes the returning paragraph, not the exact final attacks.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The dance yields to exaggerated expression
transitions.how: The E♭-major dance gives way to a six-flat key signature and Un peu moins vite. Short grace-note chords introduce a middle span in which a chromatic lyrical phrase, marked with great emotion, alternates with clipped replies. The lower part no longer simply maintains the opening’s regular dance accompaniment. Debussy makes contrasting manners of expression meet inside the same miniature, rather than smoothing the change into one continuous song.
transitions.evidence: Viewed Durand score pp. 25–27 supplies the six-flat signature, slower instruction and alternating lyrical and detached writing. The report shows quiet windows at 0:45–0:50 and its strongest change at 0:52. The timing is approximate; the key signature is not being used as a machine-derived chord label.

transitions.title: Held-back phrases release the original dance
transitions.how: The expressive middle thins and holds back, leaving space before 1° Tempo restores the three-flat signature and the dance accompaniment. Familiar syncopations recover their original setting in E♭ major. Debussy first reintroduces the pattern quietly, then lets the sharper accents and fuller sound regain their force. The pause in momentum makes the returning rhythm feel newly decisive.
transitions.evidence: Viewed score p. 27 supplies Retenez, Toujours retenu, the pause and 1° Tempo return; p. 28 carries the restored dance to its ending. The report has low levels around 1:45–1:55, a strong boundary at 2:00 and louder windows at 2:05–2:10. The passage is not bar-aligned.

composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.
